Name: Distributed Monolith
Symptom: Services require coordinated releases; changes and dependency failures propagate across boundaries
Root Cause: Tightly coupled contracts or shared data prevent services from evolving independently
Why It's Tempting: Microservices architecture promised independence but teams kept the coupling
Fix: Redraw boundaries around cohesive capabilities; keep strongly consistent operations together; use independently evolvable contracts; do not assume async messaging alone removes coupling
Related Patterns: Bounded Context, Event-Driven Architecture, API Gateway
Keywords: distributed monolith coupling deploy together cascade shared db

Name: Shared Database Integration
Symptom: Schema changes require coordination across services; long transactions can block unrelated workloads
Root Cause: Services freely access tables owned by other services and share transaction or schema dependencies
Why It's Tempting: Local ACID transactions and one database simplify consistency and operations
Fix: When independent evolution is required establish data ownership and mediate access through APIs or events; assess cross-service consistency costs before splitting; shared storage is a tradeoff rather than automatically a defect
Related Patterns: Database per Service, Event-Driven, CDC, Strangler Fig
Keywords: shared database integration coupling schema migration

Name: God Service
Symptom: Unrelated business changes contend for one release cycle; distinct capabilities cannot evolve or scale independently
Root Cause: Incremental feature additions mix domain models and responsibilities without cohesive boundaries
Why It's Tempting: Easier to add to existing service than create new infrastructure
Fix: Identify bounded contexts and ownership; separate capabilities where independent deployment or scaling justifies it; keep cohesive operations together; traffic share or service size alone is not evidence
Related Patterns: Bounded Context, Strangler Fig, Single Responsibility
Keywords: god service monolith single point failure bloated

Name: Sync-over-Async
Symptom: Thread pool starvation and rising latency under concurrent load
Root Cause: Request handlers block on asynchronous operations using methods such as Task.Result or Task.Wait
Why It's Tempting: Synchronous control flow seems simpler to reason about
Fix: Propagate async and await through the request path; locate blocking waits with thread stacks and runtime counters; verify under concurrent load; a synchronous remote protocol alone is not sync-over-async
Keywords: sync over async blocking thread pool exhaustion latency timeout

Name: Dual Writes
Symptom: Committed database changes lack events or consumers see events for rolled-back changes
Root Cause: Independent database and broker writes can succeed or fail separately
Why It's Tempting: Simpler than setting up outbox/CDC; appears to work in happy path
Fix: Commit business changes and outbox records in one local transaction; relay only committed events or use suitable CDC; handle relay redelivery with idempotent consumers and preserve required per-entity ordering
Related Patterns: Transactional Outbox, CDC, Event Sourcing, Saga
Keywords: dual writes inconsistency database broker atomicity outbox

Name: Chatty Microservices
Symptom: Many small inter-service requests dominate endpoint latency and reduce throughput
Root Cause: Fine-grained remote APIs turn one logical operation into repeated network round trips
Why It's Tempting: Remote objects are treated like local objects; small methods seem reusable
Fix: Measure downstream request counts and latency; batch related reads or expose coarse-grained operations; bound payload size; cache only when freshness permits; reassess boundaries when batching cannot remove excessive calls
Related Patterns: API Gateway, BFF, CQRS, Materialized View
Keywords: chatty microservices network latency round trip overhead

Name: Unbounded Retry
Symptom: Retries amplify overload and delay recovery; synchronized clients create traffic spikes
Root Cause: Unbounded attempts or retries at multiple layers multiply load; backoff without jitter synchronizes callers
Why It's Tempting: Retries seem like the simplest way to handle transient errors
Fix: Retry only eligible failures and safely repeatable operations; cap attempts and total elapsed time; use capped exponential backoff with jitter and a retry budget; choose one retry owner and account for SDK retries
Related Patterns: Circuit Breaker, Exponential Backoff, Dead Letter Queue
Keywords: unbounded retry thundering herd backoff jitter max attempts retry amplification budget

Name: Missing Idempotency Key
Symptom: Retrying a non-idempotent request after a lost response repeats business side effects
Root Cause: The service cannot distinguish retries of one operation from new operations
Why It's Tempting: Idempotency adds complexity; happy path works without it
Fix: Use one unique key per logical non-idempotent operation and reuse it on retries; reject mismatched parameters; return the recorded outcome; document retention and concurrent-request behavior; already idempotent operations may not need a key
Related Patterns: Idempotent Consumer, Transactional Outbox, At-Least-Once Delivery
Keywords: idempotency key duplicate retry deduplication side effect retention

Name: Premature Microservices
Symptom: Delivery slows while operational overhead and cross-service refactoring grow
Root Cause: Adopting fine-grained services before domain boundaries and operating capabilities are understood
Why It's Tempting: Independent teams and scaling appear to justify decomposition before the need is established
Fix: Consider a modular monolith or a few coarse-grained services while learning the domain; split when stable boundaries and concrete needs justify the operational cost; experienced teams with known boundaries may start with services
Related Patterns: Modular Monolith, Bounded Context, Strangler Fig
Keywords: premature microservices monolith team size operational overhead

Name: Log-and-Throw
Symptom: Multiple layers record the same fault as separate errors; diagnostic noise obscures the actual failure
Root Cause: Each catch block logs and propagates a fault without an agreed reporting owner
Why It's Tempting: Local logging seems to guarantee the failure will be visible
Fix: Choose a fault-handling boundary to record the cause and stack; propagate diagnostic context through lower layers; avoid repeated error logs for the same fault; distinct business or audit events can still be logged where they occur
Related Patterns: Error Boundary, Structured Logging, Exception Handling
Keywords: log and throw duplicate logging noise rethrow exception

Name: Generic Error Swallowing
Symptom: An operation appears successful despite failed work; state may remain partially updated
Root Cause: Catching an exception and continuing without recovery or a visible failure outcome
Why It's Tempting: Prevents crashes; makes the service appear resilient
Fix: Catch errors where recovery or translation is possible; otherwise propagate the original cause; restore state or roll back partial changes; release resources reliably; broad catches at explicit boundaries must report failure rather than silently succeed
Related Patterns: Fail Fast, Error Boundary, Circuit Breaker
Keywords: error swallowing catch all silent failure exception broad

Name: N+1 Query
Symptom: Query count grows with the number of parent records; repeated database round trips increase latency
Root Cause: Code or ORM lazy loading fetches related records separately for each parent
Why It's Tempting: Lazy access hides extra queries; small test datasets mask the cost
Fix: Inspect generated SQL and query counts; project needed fields and eagerly load or batch required relations; paginate parent results; consider split queries when joins cause excessive row duplication; measure round trips and result size
Keywords: n+1 query orm lazy load dataloader prefetch eager

Name: Secrets in Environment Variables
Symptom: Secrets can leak through environment inspection or diagnostic logs and dumps depending on platform permissions
Root Cause: Long-lived credentials are injected without controlling exposure and lifecycle; image ENV or ARG may persist secrets
Why It's Tempting: Environment injection is convenient and widely supported
Fix: Prefer runtime retrieval from a secrets manager or restricted runtime-mounted secret files; use least privilege and rotation; never bake secrets into images; if environment injection is unavoidable restrict inspection and prevent diagnostic leakage; files also require access controls
Related Patterns: Vault, KMS, Secret Rotation, Zero Trust
Keywords: secrets environment variables env var plaintext vault kms

Name: Time-Based Cache Invalidation Only
Symptom: Cached values remain stale after writes beyond the application's freshness tolerance
Root Cause: Expiration policy is treated as a consistency guarantee without accounting for external writers or cache refill behavior
Why It's Tempting: TTL is simple and can be sufficient when bounded staleness is acceptable
Fix: Define acceptable staleness per data type; update the data store before invalidating cache-aside entries; cover external writers with invalidation where needed and retain expiry as a fallback; cache-aside does not guarantee strong consistency; bypass caching when freshness is mandatory
Keywords: cache invalidation ttl stale stampede event driven

Name: Polling Instead of Events
Symptom: Frequent empty status checks waste capacity or polling intervals miss response-latency requirements
Root Cause: Polling frequency and notification mechanism are chosen without workload or client constraints
Why It's Tempting: Polling uses ordinary HTTP and avoids callback infrastructure
Fix: Use push notifications or brokers when latency and volume justify them; polling remains valid for long-running jobs or unavailable callbacks; expose a status resource and Retry-After; stop at terminal states and define timeout and cancellation behavior
Related Patterns: Event-Driven Architecture, CDC, Webhooks, Message Broker
Keywords: polling instead events webhook cdc push notification wasted resources

Name: Missing Remote Call Deadlines
Symptom: Stalled dependencies retain resources; downstream work continues after the caller gives up
Root Cause: Remote calls have no realistic deadline or each downstream hop resets the full time budget
Why It's Tempting: Defaults avoid choosing timeout values and appear to accommodate slow operations
Fix: Set explicit deadlines based on latency needs and load tests; propagate the remaining budget to downstream calls; stop spawned work when cancellation is observed; verify each client library's deadline propagation behavior
Keywords: missing timeout deadline remote call hanging resource exhaustion cancellation propagation

Name: Unbounded Work Queues
Symptom: Queue wait and memory usage grow under sustained overload; callers time out before work starts
Root Cause: Admission exceeds processing capacity without bounds on queued or in-flight work
Why It's Tempting: Buffering every request appears to avoid rejecting work during bursts
Fix: Bound queue length and in-flight concurrency using measured capacity and latency budgets; reject excess work early with an explicit overload response; discard expired request work where semantics permit; load-test overload and recovery
Keywords: unbounded queue backlog memory overload admission control backpressure load shedding

Name: Per-Request Client Construction
Symptom: Connection churn and socket exhaustion appear under load; setup costs reduce throughput
Root Cause: Each request creates and destroys a client that owns reusable connection pools
Why It's Tempting: Short object lifetimes seem to guarantee prompt cleanup
Fix: Reuse documented thread-safe clients or managed handler pools; configure connection lifetime for DNS changes; keep request-specific state out of shared mutable defaults; promptly return borrowed database connections to their pool
Related Patterns: Connection Pooling, Resource Lifecycle, Dependency Injection
Keywords: http client per request connection pooling socket exhaustion improper instantiation dns lifetime
